lesson.title: tú & usted: The T-V Line
lesson.subtitle: Informal tú vs polite usted (worn-down Vuestra Merced), greetings and social register

hook.title: How 'Your Mercy' Became Usted
hook.content: Why does Spanish use 3rd-person verb forms ('he/she wants' = quiere, 'he/she is' = está) when speaking politely to one person with usted? Because in Golden Age Spain, polite speakers didn't say 'you' directly — they addressed a stranger in the third person as Vuestra Merced ('Your Mercy / Your Grace'): 'What does Your Mercy wish?'. Over centuries of rapid speech, Vuestra Merced wore down to vuesarced → vusted → usted — keeping its 3rd-person verb forever!

pattern.title: Dropping the -s to Step from tú to usted
pattern.content: Look at how easy the verb switch is between informal tú (friends, family, peers) and formal usted (elders, strangers, respectful service): simply remove the final -s of the tú form! tú quieres → usted quiere; tú estás → usted está; tú hablas → usted habla; tú tienes → usted tiene!
pattern.linguist_note: Vuestra Merced grammaticalized into usted between the 16th and 17th centuries, paralleling Portuguese você.
pattern.trap_note: When talking ABOUT Mr. or Mrs. García, use el señor / la señora; when speaking DIRECTLY to them, drop the article: Buenos días, señor.

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: tú, usted, ¿cómo estás?, ¿cómo está usted?, señor, señora
exercises.meaning: you (informal), you (formal: 'Your Mercy'), how are you? (informal), how are you? (formal), sir / Mr., madam / Mrs.
exercises.explanation: Drop the -s from the tú verb (estás → está, quieres → quiere) to form the usted verb!

exercises.prompt: Why does 'usted' take 3rd-person verb forms (está, quiere, habla)?
options: It evolved from 'Vuestra Merced' ('Your Mercy'), a 3rd-person title
exercises.target_answer: It evolved from 'Vuestra Merced' ('Your Mercy'), a 3rd-person title
exercises.explanation: Addressing someone as 'Your Mercy' naturally used 3rd-person verbs ('How is Your Mercy?').

exercises.prompt: Assemble the formal question: 'How are you (formal)?'
exercises.explanation: ¿Cómo está usted? — drops the -s of estás and adds usted for clarity.

exercises.idea: ask politely (using usted): 'What do you want, sir?'
cues: wants (usted form of querer: drop -s from quieres) → quiere
exercises.explanation: ¿Qué quiere, señor? — dropping -s from quieres switches cleanly to polite usted.

diagnosis.cue: When addressing señor or señora directly, use the polite usted form without -s: ¿Qué quiere, señor?

exercises.prompt: Which English word-for-word blueprint mirrors Spanish '¿Cómo está usted?'?
exercises.meaning: How are you (formal)? (literal Spanish blueprint: How stands Your-Mercy?)

summary.outcome: Switch between informal tú (with -s) and formal usted (without -s) and deploy polite greetings.

use_example.english: Good morning, madam, how are you?

summary.takeaway: Drop the final -s from the tú verb (estás → está, quieres → quiere) to speak politely with usted.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([901] Addressing with Respect): practice flipping tú verbs into usted verbs in real dialogues.

twist.explanation: ¿Qué desea usted? uses desear ('to wish/desire') in the polite 3rd-person form.

tú.etymology_derivation: Latin tū — the ancient Indo-European second person singular, preserved in Shakespeare's thou.

usted.etymology_derivation: Vuestra Merced ('Your Mercy') worn down over centuries to usted. Takes 3rd-person verb forms.

hola.etymology_derivation: H is completely silent in Spanish. Cognate with English hallo/hullo.

gracias.etymology_derivation: Latin grātia ('favor, grace'). Spanish thanks are plural: 'graces to you'.

adiós.etymology_derivation: a ('to') + Dios ('God') — identical to French adieu: 'I commend you to God'.

señor.etymology_derivation: Latin senior ('older') — English senior and sire.

señora.etymology_derivation: Takes el/la when talking ABOUT them (el señor García), and no article when addressing them directly.

estar.etymology_derivation: Latin stāre ('to stand') gives English 'stand' and 'state'. Estar describes how or where something stands right now.

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.
